segments.line: By lunchtime the workers have a name for it. The
buzzing scarab. By
the afternoon, two guards walk you to the man in charge of the whole pyramid. His name
is Hemiunu. He's the king's nephew, and this pyramid is his life's work. He has been building it for years, and he
has never once seen it from above. You
hand him the controller. He
holds the screen with both hands and doesn't say a word for a very long time.
Then he starts pointing.
From the sky, the problems are easy to see. One team is dragging a stone the long way round the whole site. You
show them the shortcut.
A boat full of limestone is stuck on a sandbank in the Nile. You
fly down the river and find the deep channel. The
crew on that boat keeps a logbook. A logbook just like it, written by an inspector called
Merer, was dug up in 2013. It's
the oldest papyrus with writing on it ever found, and it's all about bringing stone to this pyramid. Then Hemiunu asks you to fly over
the corners. From above, the base is almost a perfect square.
Each side is about two hundred and thirty metres long, and none of them is off by more than the length of your hand. They did that with
ropes, sticks and the stars. A
worker's daughter called Nefer has lost her goat. You
find it in two minutes,
behind a pile of rubble, eating somebody's lunch.
After that, Nefer follows you everywhere.
She shows you how they really live. The workers here
aren't slaves. They're
paid, in bread and beer, every single day. They
live in a town right next to the pyramid, with bakeries, breweries and doctors.
Some of them are even buried beside it, with their names on their tombs. By
the end of the week, half the building site takes its lunch break when you fly, just to watch. You have
a nickname now. The one with the sky eye. And then a
golden boat arrives from the palace.
